en: Filipino farmers use a bolo, which acts as a wedge, to easily split coconuts by concentrating force on its thin edge.
Rubber tsinelas have rough soles to increase friction, preventing students from slipping on wet tiled school floors.
Gravity pulls water down Maria Cristina Falls in Mindanao, spinning turbines to generate hydroelectric power for the region.
The black sand beaches of Ilocos Norte contain magnetite, a naturally magnetic mineral that sticks to magnets.
The Tiwi Geothermal Power Plant in Albay uses steam from underground hot rocks to spin turbines and generate electricity.
Fireflies, locally called kulisap, produce their own cold light through a chemical reaction in their abdomens to attract mates.
Sound waves bounce off the limestone walls of the Puerto Princesa Underground River, creating a distinct echo for tourists.
A traditional palayok, or clay pot, conducts heat evenly from charcoal to slowly cook a delicious chicken tinola.
Sugarcane grown in Negros Occidental stores chemical energy that factories convert into bioethanol, a renewable fuel for vehicles.
The foot pedal of a traditional treadle sewing machine acts as a lever to multiply the tailor's foot force.
The smooth, streamlined body of the tawilis, a freshwater sardine in Taal Lake, reduces water friction for faster swimming.
The gravitational pull of the moon and sun causes the daily rising and falling of ocean tides in Manila Bay.
